new_statements.rule_in_words: No general word-stress rule is given; the chapter is on verb diathesis. Two incidental remarks on verbal prefix stress: inseparable prefixes (be-, ent-, er-, ver-, zer-, sometimes um-, ueber-, durch-) are unstressed, so the verb root carries the stress, whereas separable particles (an-, auf-, um-, ab-, nach-, vor-, zu-, zusammen-..) are stressed; and be-prefixation (and prefixation generally) is only well-formed on roots with initial stress. This is a morphological conditioning of stress inside prefixed verbs, not a placement rule for the lexicon at large.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For simplex (monomorphemic) words of Modern Standard German: word accent is assigned from the right edge within a window of the last three FULL syllables (reduced/schwa syllables cannot bear accent and are not counted; a consonant-initial reduced final syllable fixes accent on the last full syllable: A'gathe, Me'lone). Weight is defined through syllable cut: a full syllable is light iff open, monophthongal and smoothly cut; every other full syllable (closed, diphthongal, or abruptly cut, i.e. virtually closed by an ambisyllabic following onset as in Mississippi, Odessa) is heavy. Rules: only full syllables accentable (R1); three-syllable window (R3); a heavy penult blocks antepenultimate accent (R4: Ve'randa, Bala'laika, Cana'letto). Defaults: heavy ultima takes final accent, especially if doubly closed (N1: La'kai, ro'bust, Laby'rinth); light ultima is not accented (N2: 'Kilo, Bi'kini); a penult ending in a high vowel before an onsetless ultima is skipped (N3: 'Pavian, Al'lotria); otherwise the penult is accented (N4). For morphologically complex words accent is morphologically governed (p. 96). He adds (p. 99) that older stages of German had initial (first-syllable) accent, in contrast to the modern right-edge system, and (p. 90 fn. 7) that in Standard German only words, not syllables, carry accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary-stress placement rule. Fn. 5 (pp. 88-89): reduced syllables cannot be accented but can be rhythmically prominent ('Nebenakzent'), e.g. 'Munterere gibt es nicht' spoken as four trochees; Sec. 6 (pp. 103-104) refers to a 'rhythmische Nebenakzentstelle' ('Kän.gu.ruh, Ap.pa.'rat) and to reduction of a full syllable between two rhythmically more prominent syllables on a Liberman/Prince-Hayes metrical grid; Sec. 5 end (p. 103): word accents yield mostly trochaic or dactylic cadences.
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 19 (p. 100): exceptions to the heavy-penult rule - names 'Turandot, 'Valentin, 'Augustin (possibly contrastive initial accent, cf. grammatical terms 'Dativ, 'Genitiv, 'Nominativ which even override the three-syllable rule); compound-like words 'Ameise, 'Talisman, 'Attentat, 'Abenteuer, 'Tamerlan; country names in -stan ('Kurdistan ~ Kurdi'stan, Us'bekistan, 'Kasachstan vs Duden Kasach'stan); O'tranto heard for Duden 'Otranto. N1 exceptions: 'Tharau, 'Aaron, 'Ballast (p. 101). N2 exceptions: mainly French loans with final accent on a light ultima (I'dee, Fi'let, Fi'lou, Ra'gout, per'du, Soi'ree), final -e read as a reduced syllable (fn. 20, p. 102). N3: but Ma'ria-type counterexamples. N4: lexically learned 'Rimini, 'Modena, 'Texaco against default Bi'kini, Mo'dena (p. 103). R2-R4 and N1-N4 hold for simplicia only; derived and inflected forms follow morphological accent rules.
new_statements.identity_note: Vennemann 1991 describes Modern Standard German (Standarddeutsch) and restricts his accent rules to simplicia (monomorphemic, largely non-native words and names); morphologically complex words are said to have morphologically governed accent. Thiersch 1978 is Standard German syntax; Joswig 2005 reviews Wiese's Standard German phonology.

sources.citation: Domahs, Frank; Blessing, Katharina; Kauschke, Christina; Domahs, Ulrike (2016). Bono Bo and Fla Mingo: Reflections of speech prosody in German second graders' writing to dictation. Frontiers in Psychology 7:856.
sources.quote: Stress assignment is more complicated and largely opaque in words with non-canonical feet or in polysyllabic words. This leads to a general need for lexical specification of stress in German. However, beyond lexicalization there is accumulating evidence for a role of syllable weight in stress assignment, such that light final and closed prefinal syllables are associated with penultimate stress whereas (super) heavy final syllables, especially if combined with light prefinal syllables, lead to stress on the antepenultimate or ultimate syllable (Janßen, 2003; Janßen and Domahs, 2008; Röttger et al., 2012; Domahs et al., 2014).
sources.note: Summary statement by the Marburg group: lexical specification plus a probabilistic weight effect (light final -> penult; superheavy final -> final or antepenult). Matches the catalog's weight-hedged coding; the main study is about children's writing.

sources.citation: Domahs, Frank; Grande, Marion; Huber, Walter; Domahs, Ulrike (2014a). The direction of word stress processing in German: evidence from a working memory paradigm. Frontiers in Psychology 5:574.
sources.quote: Quantity-sensitive accounts state that the structure or weight of the final and/or prefinal syllable is a particularly important predictor of the position of main stress in German (Vennemann, 1991; Féry, 1998; Domahs et al., 2008). Quantity-insensitive accounts typically assume that the PU is the default stress position in German ... Leftward stress computation in German is supported by the fact that only one of the last three syllables (APU, PU, or U) can bear main stress ("three-syllable window," Giegerich, 1985; Vennemann, 1991; Zonneveld et al., 1999).
